title: ar or ir er, ow oi, ear air
overview:
New sounds: ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi.
These are not short and not long. They are their own sounds.
Two letters. One sound.
Do not sound them out one by one.
functions: Say the sound for each new spelling
Read a word that has one in it
Write a word that has one in it
Know where in a word each one goes
Read the new words out loud
Choose between two spellings of one sound
learningPath: Words: the new sounds and the new words.
Write the words from their sounds.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 14. The last of Book A.
These sounds are not short and not long.
They are their own sounds.
Four of them use the letter r.
Listen. Ar. Car. c. ar. Two sounds.
Not c, a, r. Two sounds only.
Next. Or. Fork. f. or. k. Three sounds.
Next. Ir. Bird. b. ir. d. Three sounds.
Next. Er. Her. h. er. Two sounds.
Now listen to those last two again.
Bird. Her. Ir and er.
They are the SAME sound.
Two spellings. One sound. That happens a lot.
You learn which word takes which by reading.
Now two more.
Ow. Cow. c. ow. Two sounds.
It is the sound you make when it hurts.
Oi. Coin. c. oi. n. Three sounds.
One sound, not two. Not o then i.
Two more you will meet in the words.
Ear. Hear. h. ear. Two sounds.
Air. Hair. h. air. Two sounds.
Hear and hair. Listen. Hear. Hair.
They look close. They are not the same.
Hear is what your ears do.
Hair is what grows on your head.
That is all of Book A.
You can read most short words in English.
Book B is next. It has no new sounds.
It has new ways to write the ones you know.
That is Unit 14. Well done.

words.example: The word car has ar in it.
practice: It is not a short a.

words.meaning: Two letters, one sound: or. The o joins an r and makes one sound.
words.example: The word fork has or in it.
practice: It is not a short o.

words.meaning: Two letters, one sound: ir. The i joins an r and makes one sound.
words.example: The word bird has ir in it.

words.meaning: Two letters, one sound: er. The e joins an r and makes one sound.

words.meaning: Two letters, one sound: oi. It sits in the middle of a word.

grammar.title: The new sounds: ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi
grammar.explanation:
These vowels are neither short nor long.
Each pair is one sound of its own.
Four of them use the letter r.
grammar.rule:
ar   as in car     c - ar
or   as in fork    f - or - k
ir   as in bird    b - ir - d
er   as in her     h - er
ow   as in cow     c - ow
oi   as in coin    c - oi - n
grammar.workedExample:
You see ar in a word.
1. Do not read two letters.
2. Read one sound.
3. Say that sound out loud.
4. Now find it in car.
5. Say the sound again there.
grammar.mistake:
Sounding out both letters gives no word at all.
car is not c - a - r.
It is c - ar.
grammar.tip: Two letters. Look once. Say once.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. ar
2. or
3. ir
4. er
5. ow
6. oi
grammar.answers:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say ONE sound each time?
Two sounds means you read the letters, not the spelling.

grammar.title: Reading a word that has ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi in it
grammar.explanation:
Find the two letters first.
Read them as one sound.
Then read the rest of the word.
grammar.rule:
car      c - ar
fork     f - or - k
bird     b - ir - d
her      h - er
cow      c - ow
coin     c - oi - n
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word fork.
1. Look for the two letters.
2. Cover them with your finger.
3. Read what is left.
4. Now put the one sound back in.
5. Join it all. fork.
grammar.mistake:
Reading left to right, letter by letter, breaks here.
Look for the pair BEFORE you start.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. c - ar
2. f - or - k
3. b - ir - d
4. h - er
5. c - ow
6. c - oi - n
grammar.answers:
1. car
2. fork
3. bird
4. her
5. cow
6. coin
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.title: Writing a word that has ar, or, ir, er, ow, oi in it
grammar.explanation:
Say the word. Break it into sounds.
One of those sounds needs TWO letters.
Count sounds, then write.
grammar.rule:
car      c - ar             2 sounds, 3 letters
fork     f - or - k         3 sounds, 4 letters
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write bird.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: b - ir - d.
3. Which sound needs two letters?
4. Write that pair together.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.mistake:
One letter for each sound is wrong now.
The new sound takes two letters.
grammar.tip: Count sounds. Some need two letters.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. bird
2. her
3. cow
4. coin
5. hear
6. hair
grammar.answers:
1. bird
2. her
3. cow
4. coin
5. hear
6. hair
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.title: ir and er say one sound
grammar.explanation:
Two spellings. One sound.
You cannot hear which one a word uses.
You learn that by reading the word.
grammar.rule:
ir    bird, girl, first, shirt
er    her, water, under, sister

Say bird. Say her. The same middle sound.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write the sound er.
1. Say the word out loud.
2. The sound does not tell you the spelling.
3. Think of the word written down.
4. If you have seen it, write what you saw.
5. If not, write er and check later.
grammar.mistake:
There is no rule here to learn.
Waiting for one keeps you stuck.
grammar.tip: Same sound. Two spellings. Read to learn which.
grammar.practice:
Say each word. Is the spelling ir or er?
1. bird
2. her
3. girl
4. under
5. first
6. water
grammar.answers:
1. ir
2. er
3. ir
4. er
5. ir
6. er
You could not hear it. You had to look. That is the point.

grammar.title: ear and air: hear and hair
grammar.explanation:
Two more pairs, both with a vowel and r.
They look close and sound close.
The meanings are not close at all.
grammar.rule:
ear   hear, near, year, clear
air   hair, fair, chair, pair

hear  what your ears do
hair  what grows on your head
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word hear.
1. Find the pair. It is ear.
2. That is one sound.
3. Say h, then ear.
4. Two sounds. Hear.
5. Now do the same with hair.
grammar.mistake:
Hear and hair get swapped constantly.
Read the whole word, not the first two letters.
grammar.tip: Ear is for ears. Air is for hair.
grammar.practice:
Which word fits? hear or hair
1. I can ___ the cow.
2. Her ___ is dark.
3. Did you ___ that?
4. Cut my ___.
5. I cannot ___ you.
6. Wash your ___.
grammar.answers:
1. hear
2. hair
3. hear
4. hair
5. hear
6. hair
All six right? You have them apart.

readings.title: The Farm
readings.genre: A short text using known sounds
readings.setting: A farm, on a cold morning
readings.passage:
I went to the farm in the car.
A cow was in the yard.
A bird sat on the cart.
I can hear the cow.
A girl fed the cow. Her hair was dark.
It was hard work on the farm.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The new sounds
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat each sound.
ar
or
ir
er
ow
oi
ONE sound each. Not two.
Now say each one three times.
Tap the mic. Say them all.
Check: one sound, or did two slip out?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say one of the new sounds. Say it back.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Read the words
speaking.instructions:
Say each word two ways. Slow, then fast.
1. c - ar ... car
2. f - or - k ... fork
3. b - ir - d ... bird
4. h - er ... her
5. c - ow ... cow
6. c - oi - n ... coin
Tap the mic. Say all six both ways.
Check: was the new spelling one sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say three sounds. Join them and say the word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it, then write it
speaking.instructions:
For each word: say it, break it, write it.
1. bird
2. her
3. cow
4. coin
5. hear
6. hair
Tap the mic. Say each word and its sounds.
Check: did you say the sounds before you wrote?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with the new spelling. Break it out loud.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Read the list
speaking.instructions:
Read these out loud, straight down the list.
car
fork
bird
her
cow
coin
hear
hair
Do it twice. The second time, try not to stop.
Tap the mic. Read the list twice.
Check: was the second time easier?
speaking.tutor: Read the list to the tutor. Ask which words were not clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — ir and er
speaking.instructions:
Say each word. Then say the spelling.
bird. her. girl. under. first. water.
Say the word, then say ir or er.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: did they all have the same middle sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say bird and her. Listen for the middle.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — hear and hair
speaking.instructions:
Say each pair out loud, one after the other.
hear, hair
near, fair
year, pair
Then use each one in a short sentence.
Tap the mic. Say all three pairs.
Check: did the two words sound different?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor: can you hear me? Then point at your hair.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Words with the new spelling
writing.prompt:
Say each word. Break it into sounds.
Write two letters for the new sound.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
The new spelling written as a pair.
You read each one back after writing it.
writing.extension: Now write one more word with the same spelling.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Sounds and letters
writing.prompt:
Write each word. Then write two numbers.
How many sounds. How many letters.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
Two numbers beside each one.
The numbers are not the same. That is the point.
writing.extension: Find a word where they ARE the same.

1.
2.
3.
4.
5.
6.

activities.instructions:
Say each word. Write ir or er.

4. under

activities.answers:

2. er
3. ir
4. er

You could not hear it. You had to look.
That is what this practice is for.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the list
activities.instructions:
Read this list out loud, twice.
car
fork
bird
her
cow
coin
hear
hair
activities.answers:
There is no written key.
Check: did you read all eight?
Was the second reading faster than the first?
Stopping on a word is normal. Try again and move on.
activities.solo: Record both readings, then listen back.

activities.title: Practice 6 — hear or hair?
activities.instructions:
Write hear or hair in each gap.
1. I can ___ the cow.
2. Her ___ is dark.
3. Did you ___ that?
4. Cut my ___.
5. I cannot ___ you.
6. Wash your ___.
activities.answers:
1. hear
2. hair
3. hear
4. hair
5. hear
6. hair
Five or more right: you have them apart.
Below five: ears hear. Heads have hair.
activities.solo: Do all six, then check together.

quizzes.q: When you see ar you should ___.
quizzes.why: Read the pair as one, not as two letters.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: c - ar. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: The sounds in order make the word.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: f - or - k. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: Find the pair first, then read the rest.

quizzes.q: To write a word with the new spelling you ___.
options: write two letters for that sound
write one letter for each sound
quizzes.a: write two letters for that sound
quizzes.why: The new sound is one sound and two letters.

quizzes.q: How many sounds are in fork?
quizzes.why: Count what you HEAR. There are more letters than sounds.

options: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.a: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.why: Letter by letter is the slow way here.

quizzes.q: You cannot read a word. What do you do first?
quizzes.why: Find the pair, then read around it.
ir and er are one sound with two spellings.

quizzes.q: How do you know a word takes ir, not er?
quizzes.why: The sound cannot tell you. Reading can.
Hearing is what your ears do.
Hair is what grows on your head.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

This is the whole unit, and it goes against everything Units 2 to 7 taught. Expect a learner to read the letters separately for a while. Do not explain it again; point at the pair and say the one sound, and have them say it back. It is a habit, and habits are built by repetition, not by argument.

teacherNotes.type: Find the pair before reading, not during
teacherNotes.note: Left-to-right letter-by-letter reading breaks on these words, because the learner commits to the first letter's sound before they have seen the second. The move is to scan the word for the pair first. A finger under the pair is enough. It looks like a crutch and it is the skill.

From here to the end of the level there are always more letters than sounds. A learner who counts letters will write a spare letter into every word. Have them say the word and count on their fingers before they write.

teacherNotes.type: ir, er and ur are one sound with three spellings
teacherNotes.note: Unit 18 adds ur, so a learner who meets ir and er here as arbitrary is ready for the third. Say plainly that the spelling cannot be heard and must be seen. Adults find this less upsetting than children do, but only if you say it outright rather than letting them discover it by getting it wrong.

teacherNotes.type: hear and hair need meaning, not phonics
teacherNotes.note: Both decode correctly and a learner can read both and still use the wrong one. Anchor them to the body: ears hear, heads have hair. The practice is a gap fill for that reason — it tests the meaning the decoding cannot reach.

teacherNotes.type: This is the end of Book A, and it is worth stopping on
teacherNotes.note: A learner who has reached here can read most one-syllable English. That is the hardest part of the whole level and it is behind them. Say so. Book B adds no new sounds at all, only new spellings for sounds they already have, and knowing that changes how the next six units feel.

assignment.title: Read and write the new words
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Say the sound for each new spelling.
Then read these words, slowly and then faster:
car, fork, bird, her, cow, coin
2. Write six of the words from their sounds.
Beside each one, write how many sounds it has.
Listen back before you finish.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written page
